{{short description|Isomorphism of commutative rings constructed in the theory of Lie algebras}}
{{distinguish|Harish-Chandra homomorphism}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Harish-Chandra isomorphism''', introduced by {{harvs|txt|last=[[Harish-Chandra]]|year=1951}},
is an [[isomorphism]] of commutative rings constructed in the theory of [[Lie algebra]]s. The isomorphism maps the [[center (ring theory)|center]] <math>\mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math> of the [[universal enveloping algebra]] <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math> of a [[reductive Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> to the elements <math>S(\mathfrak{h})^W</math> of the [[symmetric algebra]] <math>S(\mathfrak{h})</math> of a [[Cartan subalgebra]] <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> that are invariant under the [[Weyl group]] <math>W</math>.

== Introduction and setting ==
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a [[semisimple Lie algebra]], <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> its [[Cartan subalgebra]] and <math>\lambda, \mu \in \mathfrak{h}^*</math> be two elements of the [[Weight space (representation theory)|weight space]] (where <math>\mathfrak{h}^*</math> is the [[dual vector space|dual]] of <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>) and assume that a set of [[Positive root#Positive roots and simple roots|positive roots]] <math>\Phi_+</math> have been fixed. Let <math>V_\lambda</math> and <math>V_\mu</math> be [[highest weight module]]s with highest weights <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\mu</math> respectively.

=== Central characters ===
The <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-modules <math>V_\lambda</math> and <math>V_\mu</math> are representations of the [[universal enveloping algebra]] <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math> and its [[center (algebra)|center]] acts on the modules by [[scalar multiplication]] (this follows from the fact that the modules are generated by a highest weight vector). So, for <math>v \in V_\lambda</math> and <math>x \in \mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math>,
<math display = block>x\cdot v:=\chi_\lambda(x)v</math>
and similarly for <math>V_\mu</math>, where the functions <math>\chi_\lambda, \,\chi_\mu</math> are homomorphisms from <math>\mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math> to scalars called ''central characters''.

==Statement of Harish-Chandra theorem==
For any <math>\lambda, \mu \in \mathfrak{h}^*</math>, the characters <math>\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu</math> if and only if <math>\lambda + \delta</math> and <math>\mu + \delta</math> are on the same [[orbit (group theory)|orbit]] of the [[Weyl group]] of <math>\mathfrak{h}^*</math>, where <math>\delta</math> is the half-sum of the [[positive root]]s, sometimes known as the '''Weyl vector'''.{{sfn|Humphreys|1978|page=130}}

Another closely related formulation is that the [[Harish-Chandra homomorphism]] from the center of the [[universal enveloping algebra]] <math>\mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math> to <math>S(\mathfrak{h})^W</math> (the elements of the symmetric algebra of the Cartan subalgebra fixed by the Weyl group) is an [[isomorphism]].

===Explicit isomorphism===
More explicitly, the isomorphism can be constructed as the composition of two maps, one from <math>\mathfrak{Z} = \mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math> to <math>U(\mathfrak{h}) = S(\mathfrak{h}),</math> and another from <math>S(\mathfrak{h})</math> to itself.

The first is a projection <math>\gamma: \mathfrak{Z} \rightarrow S(\mathfrak{h})</math>. For a choice of positive roots <math>\Phi_+</math>, defining 
<math display=block>n^+ = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Phi_+} \mathfrak{g}_\alpha, n^- = \bigoplus_{\alpha \in \Phi_-} \mathfrak{g}_\alpha</math>
as the corresponding positive nilpotent subalgebra and negative nilpotent subalgebra respectively, due to the [[Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem]] there is a decomposition
<math display=block>U(\mathfrak{g}) = U(\mathfrak{h}) \oplus (U(\mathfrak{g})\mathfrak{n}^+ + \mathfrak{n}^-U(\mathfrak{g})).</math>
If <math>z \in \mathfrak{Z}</math> is central, then in fact 
<math display=block>z \in U(\mathfrak{h}) \oplus (U(\mathfrak{g})\mathfrak{n}^+ \cap \mathfrak{n}^-U(\mathfrak{g})).</math>
The restriction of the projection <math>U(\mathfrak{g}) \rightarrow U(\mathfrak{h})</math> to the centre is <math>\gamma: \mathfrak{Z} \rightarrow S(\mathfrak{h})</math>, and is a homomorphism of algebras. This is related to the central characters by
<math display=block>\chi_\lambda(x) = \gamma(x)(\lambda)</math>

The second map is the ''twist map'' <math>\tau: S(\mathfrak{h}) \rightarrow S(\mathfrak{h})</math>. On <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> viewed as a subspace of <math>U(\mathfrak{h})</math> it is defined <math>\tau(h) = h - \delta(h)1</math> with <math>\delta</math> the Weyl vector.

Then <math>\tilde \gamma = \tau \circ \gamma: \mathfrak{Z} \rightarrow S(\mathfrak{h})</math> is the isomorphism. The reason this twist is introduced is that <math>\chi_\lambda</math> is not actually Weyl-invariant, but it can be proven that the twisted character <math>\tilde \chi_\lambda = \chi_{\lambda - \delta}</math> is.

== Applications ==
The theorem has been used to obtain a simple Lie algebraic proof of [[Weyl's character formula]] for finite-dimensional irreducible representations.{{sfn|Humphreys|1978|pages=135–141}} The proof has been further simplified by [[Victor Kac]], so that only the quadratic Casimir operator is required; there is a corresponding streamlined treatment proof of the character formula in the second edition of {{harvtxt|Humphreys|1978|pages=143–144}}.

Further, it is a necessary condition for the existence of a non-zero homomorphism of some highest weight modules (a homomorphism of such modules preserves central character). A simple consequence is that for [[Verma module]]s or [[generalized Verma module]]s <math>V_\lambda</math> with highest weight <math>\lambda</math>, there exist only finitely many weights <math>\mu</math> for which a non-zero homomorphism  <math>V_\lambda \rightarrow V_\mu</math> exists.

==Fundamental invariants==

For <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> a simple Lie algebra, let <math>r</math> be its ''rank'', that is, the dimension of any Cartan subalgebra <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. [[H. S. M. Coxeter]] observed that <math>S(\mathfrak{h})^W</math> is isomorphic to a [[polynomial ring|polynomial algebra]] in <math>r</math> variables (see [[Chevalley–Shephard–Todd theorem]] for a more general statement). Therefore, the center of the universal enveloping algebra of a simple Lie algebra is isomorphic to a polynomial algebra. The degrees of the generators of the algebra are the degrees of the fundamental invariants given in the following table.
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center"
|-
! Lie algebra || [[Coxeter number]] ''h'' || [[Dual Coxeter number]] || Degrees of fundamental invariants
|-
| '''R''' || 0 || 0 || 1
|-
| A<sub>''n''</sub> || ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 || ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 || 2, 3, 4, ..., ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1
|-
| B<sub>''n''</sub> || 2''n'' || 2''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 || 2, 4, 6, ..., 2''n''
|-
| C<sub>''n''</sub> || 2''n'' || ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 || 2, 4, 6, ..., 2''n''
|-
| D<sub>''n''</sub> || 2''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2 || 2''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2 || ''n''; 2, 4, 6, ..., 2''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2
|-
| E<sub>6</sub> || 12 || 12 || 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12
|-
| E<sub>7</sub> || 18 || 18 || 2, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 18
|-
| E<sub>8</sub> || 30 || 30 || 2, 8, 12, 14, 18, 20, 24, 30
|-
| F<sub>4</sub> || 12 || 9 || 2, 6, 8, 12
|-
| G<sub>2</sub> || 6 || 4 || 2, 6
|}

The number of the fundamental invariants of a [[Lie group]] is equal to its rank. Fundamental invariants are also related to the [[cohomology ring]] of a Lie group. In particular, if the fundamental invariants have degrees <math>d_1, \cdots, d_r</math>, then the generators of the cohomology ring have degrees <math>2d_1-1, \cdots, 2d_r-1</math>. Due to this, the degrees of the fundamental invariants can be calculated from the [[Betti number]]s of the Lie group and vice versa. In another direction, fundamental invariants are related to cohomology of the [[classifying space]]. The cohomology ring <math>H^*(BG, \mathbb{R})</math> is isomorphic to a polynomial algebra on generators with degrees <math>2d_1, \cdots, 2d_r</math>.<ref name="borel_sur_la_cohomologie">{{cite journal |last1=Borel |first1=Armand |title=Sur la cohomologie des espaces homogenes des groupes de Lie compacts |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |date= Apr 1954 |volume=76| issue =  2| pages= 273–342 }}</ref>

==Examples==
*If <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})</math>, then the center of the universal enveloping algebra is generated by the [[Casimir invariant]] of degree 2, and the Weyl group acts on the Cartan subalgebra, which is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, by negation, so the invariant of the Weyl group is the square of the generator of the Cartan subalgebra, which is also of degree 2.
* For <math>\mathfrak{g} = A_2 = \mathfrak{sl}(3,\mathbb{C})</math>, the Harish-Chandra isomorphism says <math>\mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math> is isomorphic to a polynomial algebra of Weyl-invariant polynomials in two variables <math>h_1, h_2</math> (since the Cartan subalgebra is two-dimensional). For <math>A_2</math>, the Weyl group is <math>S_3 \cong D_6</math> which acts on the CSA in the standard representation. Since the Weyl group acts by reflections, they are isometries and so the degree 2 polynomial <math>f_2(h_1, h_2) = h_1^2 + h_2^2</math> is Weyl-invariant. The contours of the degree 3 Weyl-invariant polynomial (for a particular choice of standard representation where one of the reflections is across the x-axis) are shown below. These two polynomials generate the polynomial algebra, and are the fundamental invariants for <math>A_2</math>.
* For all the Lie algebras in the classification, there is a fundamental invariant of degree 2, the '''quadratic Casimir'''. In the isomorphism, these correspond to a degree 2 polynomial on the CSA. Since the Weyl group acts by reflections on the CSA, they are isometries, so the degree 2 invariant polynomial is <math>f_2(\mathbf{h}) = h_1^2 + \cdots + h_r^2</math> where <math>r</math> is the dimension of the CSA <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>, also known as the rank of the Lie algebra.
* For <math>\mathfrak{g} = A_1 = \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})</math>, the Cartan subalgebra is one-dimensional, and the Harish-Chandra isomorphism says <math>\mathcal{Z}(U(\mathfrak{g}))</math> is isomorphic to the algebra of Weyl-invariant polynomials in a single variable <math>h</math>. The Weyl group is <math>S_2</math> acting as reflection, with non-trivial element acting on polynomials by <math>h \mapsto -h</math>. The subalgebra of Weyl-invariant polynomials in the full polynomial algebra <math>K[h]</math> is therefore only the even polynomials, generated by <math>f_2(h) = h^2</math>.

* For <math>\mathfrak{g} = B_2 = \mathfrak{so}(5) = \mathfrak{sp}(4)</math>, the Weyl group is <math>D_8</math>, acting on two coordinates <math>h_1, h_2</math>, and is generated (non-minimally) by four reflections, which act on coordinates as <math>(h_1 \mapsto -h_1, h_2 \mapsto h_2), (h_1 \mapsto h_1, h_2 \mapsto -h_2), (h_1 \mapsto h_2, h_2 \mapsto h_1), (h_1 \mapsto -h_2, h_2 \mapsto h_1)</math>. Any invariant quartic must be even in both <math>h_1</math> and <math>h_2</math>, and invariance under exchange of coordinates means any invariant quartic can be written <math>f_4(h_1, h_2) = ah_1^4 + bh_1^2h_2^2 + ah_2^4.</math> Despite this being a two-dimensional [[vector space]], this contributes only one new fundamental invariant as <math>f_2(h_1,h_2)^2</math> lies in the space. In this case, there is no unique choice of quartic invariant as any polynomial with <math>b \neq 2a</math> (and <math>a,b</math> not both zero) suffices.

==Generalization to affine Lie algebras==
The above result holds for [[reductive Lie algebra|reductive]], and in particular [[semisimple Lie algebra]]s. There is a generalization to [[affine Lie algebra]]s shown by [[Boris Feigin|Feigin]] and [[Edward Frenkel|Frenkel]] showing that an algebra known as the Feigin–Frenkel center is isomorphic to a [[W-algebra]] associated to the [[Langlands dual]] Lie algebra <math>^L\mathfrak{g}</math>.<ref name="molev">{{cite journal |last1=Molev |first1=Alexander |title=On Segal–Sugawara vectors and Casimir elements for classical Lie algebras |journal=Letters in Mathematical Physics |date=19 January 2021 |volume=111 |issue=8 |doi=10.1007/s11005-020-01344-3 |arxiv=2008.05256 |s2cid=254795180 }}</ref><ref name="ffr">{{cite journal |last1=Feigin |first1=Boris |last2=Frenkel |first2=Edward |last3=Reshetikhin |first3=Nikolai |title=Gaudin Model, Bethe Ansatz and Critical Level |journal=Commun. Math. Phys. |date=3 Apr 1994 |volume=166 |pages=27–62 |doi=10.1007/BF02099300 |arxiv=hep-th/9402022 |s2cid=17099900 }}</ref>

The '''Feigin–Frenkel center''' of an affine Lie algebra <math>\hat \mathfrak{g}</math> is not exactly the center of the universal enveloping algebra <math>\mathcal{Z}(U(\hat \mathfrak{g}))</math>. They are elements <math>S</math> of the vacuum [[affine Lie algebra#affine vertex algebra|affine vertex algebra]] at critical level <math>k = -h^\vee</math>, where <math>h^\vee</math> is the [[coxeter element#definitions|dual Coxeter number]] for <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> which are annihilated by the positive [[loop algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}[t]</math> part of <math>\hat \mathfrak{g}</math>, that is, 
<math display=block>\mathfrak{Z}(\hat \mathfrak{g}) := \{S \in V_{\text{cri}}(\mathfrak{g}) | \mathfrak{g}[t]S = 0\}</math>
where <math>V_{\text{cri}}(\mathfrak{g})</math> is the affine vertex algebra at the critical level. Elements of this center are also known as ''singular vectors'' or ''Segal–Sugawara vectors''.

The isomorphism in this case is an isomorphism between the Feigin–Frenkel center and the W-algebra constructed associated to the Langlands dual Lie algebra by [[W-algebra#Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction|Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction]]:
<math display=block>\mathfrak{Z}(\hat \mathfrak{g}) \cong \mathcal{W}(^L\mathfrak{g}).</math>
There is also a description of <math>\mathfrak{Z}(\hat \mathfrak{g})</math> as a polynomial algebra in a finite number of countably infinite families of generators, <math>\partial^n S_i, i = 1, \cdots, l,  n \geq 0</math>, where <math>S_i, i = 1, \cdots, l</math> have degrees <math>d_i +1, i = 1, \cdots, l</math> and <math>\partial</math> is the (negative of) the natural derivative operator on the loop algebra.
